newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major denies Conservative sleaze cover-up.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major denies Conservative sleaze cover-up.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, on the ropes with an election just months away, came out fighting on Sunday with an angry rebuttal of claims that an aide tried to cover up allegations of sleaze made against a former minister.

Major, asserting his leadership ahead of a make-or-break party conference, also slapped down right-wing Conservatives who want him to rule out joining a single European currency and taunted the Labour opposition as a party that has lost its soul.

Long-running allegations that former trade minister Neil Hamilton improperly took cash in return for asking parliamentary questions took a new twist on Sunday when newspapers reported that one of Major's aides, David Willetts, had tried to influence a parliamentary investigation into the affair in 1994.
Although the chairman of the probe denied having been influenced, opposition leaders said the reports raised serious questions about possible perversion of parliamentary procedures.
But Major denounced newspapers for holding "kangaroo courts" and for twisting the truth.

"I think this constant, persistent determination to smear the longest-lived political party, that has served its country in government more often and better than any other political party in the world, is a low piece of political trickery, and I bitterly resent it," Major told BBC television.

His voice at times rising with anger, Major said he had offered the government's full cooperation with Sir Gordon Downey, the commissioner for parliamentary standards, who is investigating the affair.

"If the Government had anything to hide, would I have taken that action? he said, banging his hand on the table for emphasis. "I bitterly resent the imputation that the government are involved in trying to hide this in any way."
The cash-for-questions scandal is one of two dark clouds gathering over the Conservatives' annual conference, the last before a general election that Major must hold by May.
The other, as ever, is Europe.

Euro-sceptic Conservatives opposed to closer integration are clamouring for Major to wrap himself in the flag for the election by ruling out Britain's membership of the single European currency planned for 1999.

But Major stuck resolutely to his wait-and-see policy, insisting it would be a betrayal of Britain's national interest to shut itself out of negotiations on the terms of economic and monetary union (EMU) by ruling out joining in advance.
"The argument that we should divorce ourselves from these negotiations now has no intellectual coherence whatever... it is not credible, and it isn't going to happen," Major said.
In a further rebuff to the Euro-sceptics, the prime minister said right-wing demands for finance minister Kenneth Clarke to be sacked for his pro-European views were "nonsense".
Appealing for unity over Europe at the conference, which starts on Tuesday in the southern resort of Bournemouth, Major said: "There's no point in rows this week... it's very silly."

Major needs a good conference to have any hope of launching a fightback against Tony Blair's Labour party, which cemented its 20-point lead in opinion polls after its own gathering last week in Blackpool, hailed as the most successful in years.

"After 17 years in office, for us to win the next election is going to be an immensely difficult task on any view of it," former Conservative deputy prime minister Lord Geoffrey Howe told Sky television.
But Major said voters were deluding themselves if they believed Labour's claims to keep tax and spending low.

Labour, he said, would say and do anything to regain office: "This is a curious party these days. It seems to me that this a party that has lost its soul. People don't know what the Labour party stand for any more."
